description: Corpus for auditing Reader View extraction. Each entry is a real page, categorised by the markup problem it represents rather than by topic, so a regression shows up as a category going soft rather than as one URL breaking. `expect` records what a healthy result looks like; `note` says why the page is in the list.

sites.note: Semantic, stable markup with a long body. The easy case; if this regresses, something is badly wrong.
Docs page with a sidebar table of contents competing with the body.

Every code sample is an <mdn-code-example> custom element whose light DOM is empty and whose content lives in an open shadow root. cloneNode does not copy a shadow root, so clone-based extraction drops all twelve samples and reports success. Pins that shadow content is inlined.
Sphinx output. Heavy on code blocks, which some extractors drop.
Hugo docs with two sidebars and a feedback widget inside the content column.
Very long single-page essay with inline figures.
Nearly unstyled HTML. Almost no class names for Readability to score.
Short link-blog post. Tests that a legitimately short article is not mistaken for a truncated one.
Gatsby build with hashed class names and a very long body.
Movable Type. Comments, related posts and prev/next all share the article's column, so the generic rungs over-capture. Has a site rule.
Substack on a custom domain, so the *.substack.com rule does not apply. Hashed class names beside a few stable ones.
Long-form with inline ads, newsletter widgets and a comments link inside the body.
Engineering post, heavy on code blocks and tables.
Marketing-shaped blog with related-post rails.
News with picture/source responsive images and a support-us appeal mid-article.
React-rendered news with lazy images and a related-topics rail.
Multi-page-capable article with a heavy comment section.
Next.js with utility-class CSS. The modern-markup case Readability scores worst on.
Wire copy with an ad slot between every few paragraphs.
Hashed class names throughout, plus a member-preview gate on some posts.
Chinese SPA. Content mounts after load, so it exercises the readiness wait.

Question plus many answers — the case the thread rule exists for. Each post must come out as its own card with its author and score; the author is the LAST post-signature, since the first is the editor.

A comment tree, nested. Exercises the parts nothing else does: author, score and depth read from attributes rather than selectors, indentation from depth, and the fact that a parent comment contains its replies — so a body has to be attributed to the innermost post that holds it or the top comment repeats the whole subtree.
Every class is hashed, so the rule hangs on data-testid. The timeline is virtualised: only the rendered tweets can be extracted, so a partial thread is the expected result, not a bug.

Answers are truncated until a (more) control is clicked, so this is the one site where the rule's expand list carries most of the value — 11196 characters without it, 25557 with. The post container is selected with :has(), because the author link is a sibling of the body. Sponsored answers look exactly like real ones and come through attributed to the advertiser.
A comment thread, not an article. Table-based layout with almost no prose. Should be refused rather than half-extracted.
Link aggregator page whose body is a comment tree.
66-page PDF. Only the accessibility path can read it, and it returns the first pages while the rest is captured.
